extracted.intended_audience: architects, architecture students, art critics, and designers interested in aesthetic standards for 'living' architecture
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing or producing architecture that expresses 'life' — criteria for vitality, proportion, workmanship, imitation, and expressive irregularity as set out in Ruskin's 'The Lamp of Life'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of vital energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Things (and especially architectural creations) are noble or ignoble in proportion to the fulness of the life which either they themselves enjoy, or of whose action they bear the evidence; architecture depends in the utmost degree upon the vivid expression of the intellectual life which has been concerned in their production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for visible signs that the builder's or designer's intellect and energy have been actively engaged in the work. A building should show 'sensation in every inch' rather than inert, merely decorative composition. Anti-pattern: perfectly made inert objects that lack any trace of creative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic (true) life vs false life
rubrics_metrics.description: True life is the independent force which assimilates and governs external things; false life is a life of custom and accident, crystallised habits and hollow routine which only imitate living powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether architecture manifests an inward purposive will (true life) rather than mere conventional forms or habit. Signs of false life include formulaic repetition, hollow adherence to precedent, and work ‘overlaid’ with habit. Aim for designs that actively judge and transform materials and context rather than merely follow fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthy imitation (not borrowing without paying interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no sign of deadness that an art borrows or imitates, but it is a sign if it 'borrows without paying interest' or imitates without choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowed elements are acceptable so long as they are consciously transformed and subordinated to the new style's life. Anti-pattern: slavish copies that add nothing and show no internal power of transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frankness in imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Vital imitation is marked by frankness: there is never any effort to conceal the sources of its borrowing; the copyist acknowledges and openly accepts them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open homage or visible borrowing suggests confidence and internal power. Examples: Raffaelle carrying off whole figures from Masaccio; Romanesque architects gathering columns and capitals where they could find them. Hidden or furtive imitation suggests weakness or lack of creative force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audacity of treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinguishing character of vital imitation is audacity — the unhesitating and sweeping sacrifice of precedent where precedent becomes inconvenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise bold departures from precedent when they solve problems and fulfil the work's instincts (example: Pisan adaptation of columns into pedimental space). Anti-pattern: timid, precedent-bound solutions that avoid necessary innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of execution to conception (progressive contempt of refinement)
rubrics_metrics.description: In advancing schools there is often a visible subordination of execution to conception: a neglect or contempt of refinement in execution that shows impatience and creative urgency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value work where conception leads and minute execution is willingly subordinated when necessary; this is not sloppiness but a mark of development and energetic forward-movement. However, do not conflate this with permanent carelessness — perfect finish still belongs to perfected art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finish in the right place; workmanship must not out-run design
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect and delicate finish is characteristic of high schools, but a 'progressive finish' belongs to progressive art; a fatal sign is workmanship having 'gone ahead of the design.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether finishing details serve the conception and overall life of the work. Avoid over-finishing trivial parts at the expense of the whole; equally, ensure that lack of finish is not mere incompetence. Ruskin reserves the right to ask 'what is finish? and what is its right place?' — apply context-sensitive judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impatience and energetic sketching
rubrics_metrics.description: A living architecture often shows impatience — hurried, sketch-like handling in subordinate parts (e.g., 'sculptural sketching') that corresponds to the master's bold conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize sketchy or variable execution (lines sometimes deep, sometimes shallow, sometimes broken off) as deliberate expressive economy when it harmonizes with a strong overall idea (example: Nicolo Pisano's arch mouldings). Anti-pattern: sketchiness that obscures form or looks like incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance for imperfect symmetry and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Contempt of exact symmetry and measurement is a sign of a vigorous, developing architecture; early schools often accept unequal measurements because feeling, not rule, governed them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value subtle asymmetries and minor irregularities that enhance life and variety. Anti-pattern: slavish insistence on numerical symmetry when it would deaden the composition; conversely, do not mistake random errors for purposeful variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visible evidence of creative struggle and transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Living architecture often contains traces of struggle — borrowed carved blocks integrated and re-expressed, distorted stones neatly fitted, and other marks showing adaptation rather than mere copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for transformed reused elements and for the compositional evidence that the builder synthesized materials into a unified thought. These marks are positive when they indicate active reworking; they are negative when they result from neglect or incompetence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptive proportioning and accommodation to necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Living Architecture accommodates to every architectural necessity with determined variation in arrangement, echoing organic proportioning rather than rigid regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether proportions vary to meet structural, visual, or contextual needs (examples: the complex proportional schemes of Pisa and St. Mark's where arches and shafts vary in size and relationships). Criterion favors adaptive, context-responsive proportion over monotonous equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of deliberate distortion to achieve visual effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Builders sometimes employ distortion (e.g., sloping foliage shields, altered shaft heights, oblique panels) to conceal defects or to correct optical or structural issues; such devices can be constructive parts of living design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge distortions by intention and result: are they conscious devices that enhance composition (example: Pisan columns exaggerated to conceal leaning walls), or are they accidental faults? Constructive distortions should be neat and integrated, not clumsy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex hierarchical variety (alternation and unequal repetition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Varied alternation (e.g., seven arches arranged in subtle alternating proportions, differing arcade heights in arithmetical progression) produces harmony and life rather than monotony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer schemes with hierarchical variation (central larger, flanking pairs unequal in alternating order, different arcades having different heights and numbers) that create musical-like interplay of ascending and descending proportions. Anti-pattern: rigid repetition of identical bays producing flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction from feeling rather than explicit rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Many great medieval builders worked 'from feeling' rather than conscious mathematical principles; the result is marvellous life and subtlety in arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value designs that appear to have been governed by aesthetic feeling and organic growth. When teaching or designing, encourage sensibility alongside knowledge of rules — feeling can produce subtle life that formulas cannot.
